Reproducing Tingley et al. (2021) from dandiset 000233¶

Paper. Tingley D, McClain K, Kaya E, Carpenter J, Buzsáki G (2021). A metabolic function of the hippocampal sharp wave-ripple. Nature 597, 82-86. doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03811-w. The claims file was written from the accepted author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC9214835) with its Methods, Extended Data legends and Supplementary Information.

Dandiset. DANDI:000233, version 0.250624.0414. The paper cites no DANDI version (its data statement points to the lab's server). This is the most recent published version; the earlier one, 0.230223.0815, lists the same 345 files with the same sizes, so the choice does not change the data.

What the dandiset holds. 345 NWB files from 25 rats: CA1 LFP at 1,250 Hz, tables of detected SPW-Rs, the iPro2 glucose sensor current, a head accelerometer, and sleep states for six rats. It holds no spike units, no optogenetic stimulation times, no CNO or vehicle labels and injection times, no meal times, and no cohort labels, so the optogenetic, DREADD, fasting and unit claims cannot be tested.

Random numbers are drawn only for circular shuffles, with a fixed seed in each claim's section.

Data check¶

The archive's metadata and the files are checked against each other and against the paper's description. Each check is stated under its output.

No file holds spike units, optogenetic stimulation times, injection times or labels (CNO or vehicle), meal times, or a cohort label: only the files of CGM1 name their experiment ("ripple/glucose recording", surgery rCA1), the rest point to Supplementary Table 1, whose rats are numbered 1 to 45 while the dandiset's subjects are named CGM1 to CGM60, bruce, dt15, flex1, ros and Vanessa, with no mapping between the two. SPW-R tables come under seven names; the dorsal and ventral tables identify the dorsal and ventral rats. The full description strings say no more: session_description is "no description" or points to Supplementary Table 1, and subject/description is the paper's count of 45 rats over all cohorts, the same in every file. /intervals is absent, /stimulus/presentation, /stimulus/templates and /analysis are empty in every file, /processing holds only the LFP, the SPW-R tables and (six subjects) sleep states, and the electrode tables name channels by number with location "unknown", so no file holds a stimulation, TTL or condition channel. The SPW-R tables carry no attributes beyond their column names and description: the detection parameters the Methods say are stored with each session's ripple events (in the lab's MATLAB files) are not in the NWB files.

rows = []
for f in kept:
    named = S.file_start_from_name(f["path"])
    on_clock = S.reference_time(f["reference"]) + pd.Timedelta(seconds=f["lfp_t0"])
    row = {"subject": f["subject"], "name_minus_clock_s": (on_clock - named).total_seconds() if named else np.nan}
    for k, t in f["tables"].items():
        if len(t):
            row["start_minus_t0_plus_peak_s"] = float(np.median(t.start_time - (f["lfp_t0"] + t.peak)))
            row["peak_max_minus_duration_s"] = float(t.peak.max() - f["lfp_n"] / f["lfp_rate"])
    rows.append(row)
ck = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("files whose name has no date:", ck.name_minus_clock_s.isna().sum(),
      "; |file-name time - session clock| max (s):", ck.name_minus_clock_s.abs().max())
print("SPW-R start_time - (LFP start + peak), s: ", ck.start_minus_t0_plus_peak_s.describe()[["min", "50%", "max"]].round(4).to_dict())
print("last SPW-R peak - file duration, s (<= 0 means peaks are within the file):",
      round(ck.peak_max_minus_duration_s.max(), 3))
ev_all = pd.concat([t.assign(subject=f["subject"], table=k) for f in kept for k, t in f["tables"].items()])
print("share of stored CA1 events below 5 s.d. per subject:",
      {s_: round(float((g.peak_normed_power < 5).mean()), 3) for s_, g in ev_all[ev_all.table.isin(S.CA1_TABLES)].groupby("subject")})
print(ev_all.groupby("table").agg(events=("peak", "size"), min_normed_power=("peak_normed_power", "min"),
      min_duration_ms=("duration", lambda x: 1000 * x.min()), max_duration_ms=("duration", lambda x: 1000 * x.max()),
      median_frequency=("peak_frequency", "median"), min_frequency=("peak_frequency", "min"),
      max_frequency=("peak_frequency", "max")).round(2).to_string())

The date and time in each file name equals the session reference time plus the LFP starting time, so the session clock is the lab's wall clock (the reference is labelled UTC but holds local time). In the SPW-R tables, start_time is on the session clock and peak is relative to the start of the file (start_time is LFP start + peak minus 10 to 45 ms, the time from start to peak); the column descriptions do not say this. SPW-R times used here are LFP start + peak. Durations lie in 20 to 200 ms, inside the Methods' 15 to 250 ms. The Methods set the peak threshold at 5 s.d.; the stored peak normed power is at least 5 in the tables of 12 subjects but goes down to 4 in nine others (7 to 29% of their events) and below 1 in CGM30, so those tables were made with a lower threshold. The analysis keeps events of at least 5 s.d. (Methods) and shows the main results with all stored events as a variant.

ss = pd.concat([f["sleep"].assign(subject=f["subject"]) for f in kept if f["sleep"] is not None])
print("sleep-state labels:", ss.label.value_counts().to_dict(), " subjects:", sorted(ss.subject.unique()))
# clock check between SPW-Rs and sleep states: SPW-R rate per state, true and with states shifted by 30 min
rows = []
for f in kept:
    if f["sleep"] is None or not len(f["sleep"]) or S.ca1_table(f) is None:
        continue
    e = S.ripple_events(f).t.values
    for shift in (0, 1800):
        for lab, g in f["sleep"].groupby("label"):
            st, sp = g.start.values + shift, g.stop.values + shift
            n = sum(((e >= a) & (e < b)).sum() for a, b in zip(st, sp))
            rows.append({"subject": f["subject"], "shift_s": shift, "state": lab, "events": n, "s": (sp - st).sum()})
r = pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby(["subject", "shift_s", "state"]).sum()
r["per_min"] = 60 * r.events / r.s
print(r.per_min.unstack("state").round(2).to_string())

Sleep states are present for six subjects. In CGM1, CGM2, CGM3 and flex1, SPW-Rs occur at 18 to 21 per minute in NREM sleep against 3 to 12 when awake with the states as stored, and the contrast shrinks when the states are shifted by 30 min, so the SPW-R tables and the sleep states share a clock there. In dt15 the contrast is small (5.9 against 5.5 per minute) and the check does not establish it; bruce has no SPW-R table.

glucose description: Raw current from Medtronic iPro2 ISIG tracking.

Each subject's glucose series is stored whole in every one of its files. In CGM1, CGM2 and CGM3 one file stores it in a different order or relative to a different session reference time (CGM2 and CGM3 have two reference times), but on the wall clock every file holds the same readings. Times are therefore put on one clock per subject, that of its first file (helper clock_offset); the series of the first file is used. Readings are 5 min apart (300 s; a few at 301 and 302 s). The values are called nA, and their range (about 0 to 120) is consistent with the sensor current. In twelve subjects the timestamps are out of order and the series jumps by about a month at each midnight: dates whose day is 12 or less were stored with day and month swapped (a reading of 4 March 2021 is stored as 3 April). Swapping them back joins the pieces into runs of consecutive 5-min readings (fewer breaks, table above) that overlap the electrophysiology. The repair is applied to a subject only when it reduces the breaks. In CGM32 it does not (10 breaks either way): 86 readings are dated more than 30 days from the subject's median date (up to 2021-12-02), which looks like 1 to 12 February with day and month swapped, and they are left as stored. No CGM32 recording falls on those days, and the glucose-only analyses below use runs of at least 24 h, so they do not use them; the effect of the repair on the SPW-R and glucose correlation is shown below.

Eighteen subjects have CA1 SPW-Rs and glucose recorded at the same time. In CGM36, bruce and ros no file has a SPW-R table; in CGM37, CGM60, dt15 and flex1 the glucose readings and the electrophysiology cover different days. Glucose and electrophysiology share no event that could show their clocks agree independently of the claims; the repair of the dates, which brings the two into overlap, is consistent with the file names but the alignment within a day is taken as stored.

fig2-ripple-rate-predicts-glucose¶

SPW-R rate is negatively correlated with future changes in interstitial glucose, with a mean peak correlation of R = -0.21 (+- 0.08) at a lag of 10.7 (+- 4.5) min, over 30 rats.

Readings, as the claims file lists them: delta current from the raw readings (a) or after a high-pass filter (b, a centred 24-h running mean subtracted within each run, a standard choice for the cutoff the paper does not give); Pearson or Spearman correlation; one correlogram per rat (a) or one per session averaged per rat (b; a session is a file, used when it holds at least 6 h of bins, a standard choice); the lag searched over 0 to +100 min (a) or -100 to +100 min (b); all rats with SPW-Rs and glucose together (a) or the ripple and glucose cohort (b; only CGM1 is labelled as such in the files). Reading (a) leaves out CNO days and the stimulation periods of the optogenetic rats; the files label neither, so every day of every rat is used. The paper does not say how the SPW-R count of a 5-min bin is aligned with the glucose change; the main analysis pairs the count and the change over the same interval (an assumption), and the two alignments one reading earlier or later are shown as variants.

def highpass(b, hours=24):
    out = b.copy()
    w = int(hours * 12)
    out["nA"] = b.nA - b.groupby("run").nA.transform(lambda x: x.rolling(w, center=True, min_periods=1).mean())
    same = out.run.eq(out.run.shift(1))
    out["delta"] = np.where(same, out.nA - out.nA.shift(1), np.nan)
    return out

def per_session(b, iv, min_bins=72):
    """Rows of b inside each file, one table per file with at least min_bins bins of both."""
    out = []
    for x, y in iv:
        sel = b[(b.t - S.STEP >= x) & (b.t <= y)]
        if (np.isfinite(sel.rate) & np.isfinite(sel.delta)).sum() >= min_bins:
            out.append(sel)
    return out

LAG_MIN = S.LAGS * 5
# the other alignments of the SPW-R interval and the glucose change, one reading apart, are the same
# pairs at a lag one reading shorter (SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading) or longer (delta to the next reading)
ALIGN = {"same interval (main)": 0, "SPW-Rs after the reading": -1, "delta to the next reading": 1}
CC = {}
for s in RATS:
    d = SUBJ[s]
    for dname, bb in (("raw", d["b"]), ("highpass", highpass(d["b"]))):
        for m in ("pearson", "spearman"):
            CC[(s, dname, m, "rat")] = S.xcorr(bb, method=m)
            sess = per_session(bb, d["iv"])
            CC[(s, dname, m, "session")] = (np.nanmean([S.xcorr(x, method=m) for x in sess], axis=0)
                                            if sess else np.full(len(S.LAGS), np.nan))

def peak(cc, lag_range):
    sel = LAG_MIN >= 0 if lag_range == "0..+100" else np.ones(len(LAG_MIN), bool)
    if np.all(np.isnan(cc[sel])):
        return np.nan, np.nan
    i = np.nanargmin(np.where(sel, cc, np.nan))
    return cc[i], LAG_MIN[i]

rows = []
for (s, dname, m, unit), cc in CC.items():
    for lr in ("0..+100", "-100..+100"):
        R, lag = peak(cc, lr)
        rows.append({"rat": s, "delta": dname, "corr": m, "unit": unit, "lags": lr, "R": R, "lag_min": lag,
                     "R_at_10": cc[LAG_MIN == 10][0]})
PEAKS = pd.DataFrame(rows)

def summarise(df):
    return pd.Series({"rats": df.R.notna().sum(), "mean_R": df.R.mean(), "sd_R": df.R.std(),
                      "mean_lag": df.lag_min.mean(), "sd_lag": df.lag_min.std(),
                      "rats_R_negative": (df.R < 0).sum(), "R_ok": abs(df.R.mean() + 0.21) <= 0.08,
                      "lag_ok": abs(df.lag_min.mean() - 10.7) <= 4.5})
tab_a = PEAKS.groupby(["delta", "corr", "unit", "lags"]).apply(summarise)
tab_a.insert(0, "rats_set", "a: all")
tab_b = PEAKS[PEAKS.rat == "CGM1"].groupby(["delta", "corr", "unit", "lags"]).apply(summarise)
tab_b.insert(0, "rats_set", "b: CGM1")
T1 = pd.concat([tab_a, tab_b]).reset_index()
T1["both_hold_and_most_negative"] = T1.R_ok & T1.lag_ok & (T1.rats_R_negative > T1.rats / 2)
print(T1.round(3).to_string())

main = PEAKS[(PEAKS["delta"] == "raw") & (PEAKS["corr"] == "spearman") & (PEAKS.unit == "rat") & (PEAKS.lags == "-100..+100")]

print(main.merge(cov[["subject", "hours_with_both"]], left_on="rat", right_on="subject")[["rat", "hours_with_both", "R", "lag_min", "R_at_10"]].round(3).to_string())
for minh in (6, 12, 24):
    keep = cov[cov.hours_with_both >= minh].subject
    x = PEAKS[PEAKS.rat.isin(keep)].groupby(["delta", "corr", "unit", "lags"]).apply(summarise)
    print(f"rats with at least {minh} h of both: combinations where both values hold: {int((x.R_ok & x.lag_ok).sum())} of {len(x)};"
          f" raw/spearman/rat/-100..+100: R {x.loc[('raw', 'spearman', 'rat', '-100..+100'), 'mean_R']:.3f},"
          f" lag {x.loc[('raw', 'spearman', 'rat', '-100..+100'), 'mean_lag']:.1f} min, rats {int(x.loc[('raw', 'spearman', 'rat', '-100..+100'), 'rats'])}")
keep6 = cov[cov.hours_with_both >= 6].subject
x6 = PEAKS[PEAKS.rat.isin(keep6)].groupby(["delta", "corr", "unit", "lags"]).apply(summarise)
print("with at least 6 h of both, the combinations where both values hold:", list(x6[x6.R_ok & x6.lag_ok].index))
print("median of the per-rat lags (min) and rats with the peak at +5 to +15 min, all rats:")
print(PEAKS.groupby(["delta", "corr", "unit", "lags"]).lag_min.agg(
    median_lag="median", rats="count", rats_5_to_15=lambda x: int(x.between(5, 15).sum())).to_string())
passing = T1[(T1.rats_set == "a: all") & T1.both_hold_and_most_negative]
for _, r_ in passing.iterrows():
    sel = PEAKS[(PEAKS["delta"] == r_["delta"]) & (PEAKS["corr"] == r_["corr"]) & (PEAKS.unit == r_.unit) & (PEAKS.lags == r_.lags)]

# variant: other alignments of the SPW-R interval and the glucose change, one reading apart
for name, how in (("SPW-R rate over the 5 min after each reading", "rate"), ("delta to the next reading", "delta")):
    al = []
    for s in RATS:
        for dname in ("raw", "highpass"):
            bb = SUBJ[s]["b"] if dname == "raw" else highpass(SUBJ[s]["b"])
            bb = bb.copy()
            bb[how] = bb.groupby("run")[how].shift(-1)
            for m in ("pearson", "spearman"):
                cc = S.xcorr(bb, method=m)
                for lr in ("0..+100", "-100..+100"):
                    R, lag = peak(cc, lr)
                    al.append({"rat": s, "delta": dname, "corr": m, "lags": lr, "R": R, "lag_min": lag})
    t_al = pd.DataFrame(al).groupby(["delta", "corr", "lags"]).apply(summarise)
    print(f"Alignment variant, {name} (one correlogram per rat, all rats):")
    print(t_al.round(3).to_string())
# variant: all stored events, without the Methods' 5 s.d. threshold
va = []
for s in RATS:
    for m in ("pearson", "spearman"):
        cc = S.xcorr(SUBJ[s]["b_all"], method=m)

            va.append({"rat": s, "corr": m, "lags": lr, "R": R, "lag_min": lag})

plotted R range -0.593 to 0.509; colour scale -0.4 to 0.4, 15 values outside it; median correlogram minimum -0.108 at 5 min

Result: reproduced, with 18 rats where the paper has 30, under 3 of the 16 combinations of readings, resting on an assumption about the alignment. With Pearson correlation, one correlogram per rat and lags searched over -100 to +100 min, the mean peak correlation is -0.176 (raw delta current) or -0.180 (high-pass) at a mean lag of 14.2 or 14.4 min, inside both tolerances; with Spearman correlation, one correlogram per session and the high-pass delta, -0.184 at 8.8 min. The peak is negative in every rat. Mean R lies within the tolerance under all 16 combinations (-0.159 to -0.216); the mean lag does not under the other 13 (15.8 to 33.1 min), and it is unstable: the lags of single rats spread with an s.d. of 26 to 42 min, and leaving out the rats with less than 6 h of data leaves 1 combination of 16 that matches. With at least 6 h of both per rat, only the high-pass, Spearman, per-session, -100 to +100 min combination matches. The median of the per-rat lags is 5 to 15 min in every combination, but only 7 to 10 rats of 16 or 18 peak between +5 and +15 min; in the raw, Pearson, per-rat combination single-rat lags run from -100 to +80 min, and the mean lies in tolerance because peaks at -100 to -20 min offset peaks at +55 to +80 min. "R is negative in most rats" holds by construction, as R is the minimum over 41 offsets. The median correlogram has its minimum, -0.108, at +5 min. CGM1, the one rat labelled as the ripple and glucose cohort, peaks at +5 min with R -0.101 (Pearson) or -0.194 (Spearman). The outcome rests on pairing the SPW-R count and the glucose change of the same 5-min interval, an assumption: counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading moves every lag by +5 min, and then none of the 8 per-rat combinations matches (mean lags 19.2 to 37.8 min), while taking the change to the next reading moves them by -5 min and 4 of 8 match (mean lags 9.4 to 10.8 min).

fig2ef-correlation-beyond-shuffle¶

The correlation between SPW-R rate and glucose change at a 10-min lag is more negative than the correlations obtained when SPW-R rate is circularly permuted.

Per rat, the correlation at +10 min against 100 circular shuffles of SPW-R rate within each run (the claims file's shuffle), with the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test the claims file names. Both correlation types are shown.

The main analysis pairs the SPW-R count and the glucose change of the same 5-min interval, as in fig2-ripple-rate-predicts-glucose (an assumption). The two alignments one reading apart are shown as variants: counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading, or taking the change to the next reading, which is the same as moving the offset by one reading.

Result: reproduced. At +10 min the observed per-rat correlations have a median of -0.106 (Spearman; 16 of 18 rats negative) against 0.005 for 1,799 circular shuffles, KS p = 4.0e-06; with Pearson, -0.076 against 0.002, KS p = 1.5e-04. Seven rats (Spearman) lie below all 100 of their own shuffles.

The result does not depend on the alignment. Counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading, the Spearman median is -0.108 (KS p = 2.5e-07; Pearson p = 7.6e-04); taking the change to the next reading, -0.047 (KS p = 2.5e-03; Pearson p = 6.0e-03), each against its own shuffles.

fig2g-clustered-ripples¶

Isolated SPW-Rs have little or no effect on glucose, whereas clustered SPW-Rs (more than 30 per minute) are followed by a several-fold larger decrease.

As the Fig. 2g legend: the mean delta current 10 min after each 5-min epoch, grouped by the number of SPW-Rs in the epoch, pooled over rats. Clustered is more than 150 SPW-Rs per epoch (a) or more than 30 (b); isolated is 1 to 5 per epoch (claims file).

The main analysis pairs the SPW-R count and the glucose change of the same 5-min interval, as in fig2-ripple-rate-predicts-glucose (an assumption). The two alignments one reading apart are shown as variants: counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading, or taking the change to the next reading, which is the same as moving the offset by one reading.

none = ep[ep["count"] == 0]

    t = stats.ttest_ind(cl.delta_10, iso.delta_10, equal_var=False)

        cl_ = ev_[ev_["count"] > thr].d10
        print(f"   {name}, > {thr} per epoch: clustered mean {cl_.mean():.4f} nA (n = {len(cl_)}), isolated {iso_.mean():.4f} nA (n = {len(iso_)}); "
              f"ratio {cl_.mean() / iso_.mean():.2f}; Welch p = {stats.ttest_ind(cl_, iso_, equal_var=False).pvalue:.2g}")
    cur = ev_.groupby(pd.cut(ev_["count"], bins), observed=True).d10.mean()
    print(f"      curve by count: {np.round(cur.values, 3)}")

Result: reproduced under reading (a), resting on the alignment assumption. Epochs with more than 150 SPW-Rs are followed 10 min later by a mean delta current of -0.191 nA (585 epochs, 13 rats), against +0.050 nA after epochs with 1 to 5 SPW-Rs (1,718 epochs): negative and 3.9 times the magnitude, though the difference is not significant by a Welch test (p = 0.059). Under reading (b), more than 30 per epoch, the mean is -0.032 nA, smaller in magnitude than the isolated value, so (b) does not match. The curve over epoch counts is not monotonic (the 120 to 150 group is +0.125 nA), and in 3 of the 13 rats with clustered epochs their mean is not negative. Under the alignments one reading apart, counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading gives -0.102 nA after clustered epochs against -0.011 nA after isolated ones (reading (a), Welch p = 0.66), which still matches, while taking the change to the next reading gives +0.018 against -0.027 nA under (a) and -0.022 against -0.027 nA under (b), which does not.

edfig4-ripple-features¶

Of the SPW-R features, the inter-SPW-R interval (clustering) most strongly modulates the glucose effect, then amplitude, then duration, and ripple frequency least.

For each SPW-R, the delta current of the reading 10 min after the 5-min interval holding it, as in the Extended Data Fig. 4b legend; SPW-Rs pooled over rats and binned by the percentile of each feature (deciles, a; 5-percentile bins, b). Features from the Methods: amplitude is the maximum normalized squared signal (peak_normed_power), duration is stop minus start, frequency is peak_frequency, and the inter-SPW-R interval is the time from the previous SPW-R in the same file (the claims file does not say previous or next; previous is a standard choice). The influence of a feature is the range of the bin means (claims file).

The main analysis pairs the SPW-R count and the glucose change of the same 5-min interval, as in fig2-ripple-rate-predicts-glucose (an assumption). The two alignments one reading apart are shown as variants: counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading, or taking the change to the next reading, which is the same as moving the offset by one reading.

evs = []
for s in RATS:
    d = SUBJ[s]
    e = d["ev"].copy()
    e["interval"] = e.groupby("file").t.diff()
    b = d["b"].copy()
    b["delta_10"] = b.groupby("run").delta.shift(-2)
    for name, k in ALIGN.items():
        b[f"d10 {name}"] = b.groupby("run").delta.shift(-(2 + k))
    b = b[np.isfinite(b.rate)]
    # the reading whose 5-min interval holds the SPW-R: the first reading at or after it
    idx = np.searchsorted(b.t.values, e.t.values, side="left")
    ok = idx < len(b)
    idx = np.where(ok, idx, 0)
    inside = ok & (b.t.values[idx] - e.t.values < S.STEP)
    e["delta_10"] = np.where(inside, b.delta_10.values[idx], np.nan)
    for name in ALIGN:
        e[f"d10 {name}"] = np.where(inside, b[f"d10 {name}"].values[idx], np.nan)
    e["rat"] = s
    evs.append(e[np.isfinite(e.delta_10)])

Result: partially reproduced, resting on the alignment assumption. With deciles (a), the inter-SPW-R interval has the largest range of the +10-min effect across bins (0.070 nA), then duration (0.069), frequency (0.053) and amplitude (0.040), so the interval leads but the rest of the order differs. With 5-percentile bins (b), duration (0.0967) and interval (0.0966) are tied ahead of amplitude (0.061) and frequency (0.060). Per rat, amplitude has the largest range in 7 of 18 rats and the interval in 6. Resampling rats (1,000 bootstraps, decile edges fixed), the interval has the largest range in 64.7% of resamples and the full order interval > amplitude > duration > frequency occurs in 1.5%. The decile with the shortest intervals has the least negative effect (+0.004 nA, against -0.027 nA for the longest), the opposite direction to fig2g-clustered-ripples. Under the alignments one reading apart, taking the change to the next reading keeps the interval first with deciles (0.056 nA, then duration 0.043), so the outcome is the same; counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading puts the interval last under both bin widths (deciles: frequency 0.060, duration 0.047, amplitude 0.047, interval 0.031), which matches neither case of the criterion.

fig2h-phase-reset¶

The phase dispersion of the glucose rhythm decreases after SPW-Rs, more so for higher SPW-R rates.

As the claims file: glucose phase is the Hilbert phase of delta current band-passed at periods of 15 to 75 min (a) or 15 to 90 min (b) (second-order Butterworth, zero phase, within each run of at least 24 h, a standard choice); peaks are local maxima of SPW-R rate; peaks are pooled over rats and grouped into deciles of peak rate; for each decile the circular s.d. of glucose phase is taken at offsets -100 to +100 min; the decrease is the baseline (offset 0, a; mean over -100 to 0 min, b) minus the minimum from 0 to +30 min. As the minimum over seven offsets favours a decrease, the baselines minus the mean over 0 to +30 min are shown as a variant.

In [16]:
FS = 1 / S.STEP

def band_phase(b, lo_min, hi_min, col="delta", min_len=288):
    """Hilbert phase and envelope of `col` band-passed between periods lo_min and hi_min, per run."""
    ph = np.full(len(b), np.nan); env = np.full(len(b), np.nan)
    sos = signal.butter(2, [1 / (hi_min * 60), 1 / (lo_min * 60)], btype="band", fs=FS, output="sos")
    vals = b[col].values
    for _, idx in b.groupby("run").indices.items():
        x = vals[idx]
        if len(idx) < min_len:
            continue
        x = np.where(np.isfinite(x), x, np.nanmean(x))
        z = signal.hilbert(signal.sosfiltfilt(sos, x - x.mean()))
        ph[idx] = np.angle(z); env[idx] = np.abs(z)
    return ph, env

def circ_sd(a):
    a = a[np.isfinite(a)]
    if len(a) < 3:
        return np.nan
    return np.sqrt(-2 * np.log(np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * a)))))

OFFS = np.arange(-20, 21)
for band in ((15, 75), (15, 90)):
    pk = []
    for s in RATS:
        b = SUBJ[s]["b"]
        ph, _ = band_phase(b, *band)
        r = b.rate.values
        for _, idx in b.groupby("run").indices.items():
            rr = np.where(np.isfinite(r[idx]), r[idx], -1)
            peaks, _ = signal.find_peaks(rr)
            for p in peaks:
                if not np.isfinite(r[idx][p]):
                    continue
                row = np.full(len(OFFS), np.nan)
                for j, o in enumerate(OFFS):
                    if 0 <= p + o < len(idx):
                        row[j] = ph[idx][p + o]
                if np.isfinite(row[OFFS == 0][0]):
                    pk.append((s, r[idx][p], row))
    rates = np.array([x[1] for x in pk]); P = np.array([x[2] for x in pk])
    dec = pd.qcut(pd.Series(rates).rank(method="first"), 10, labels=False).values
    tab = []
    for k in range(10):
        csd = np.array([circ_sd(P[dec == k, j]) for j in range(len(OFFS))])
        post = csd[(OFFS >= 0) & (OFFS <= 6)].min()
        tab.append({"decile": k + 1, "peaks": int((dec == k).sum()), "median_rate": np.median(rates[dec == k]),
                    "csd_0": csd[OFFS == 0][0], "csd_pre_mean": csd[OFFS <= 0].mean(), "min_0_30": post,
                    "decrease_a": csd[OFFS == 0][0] - post, "decrease_b": csd[OFFS <= 0].mean() - post,
                    "decrease_a_mean": csd[OFFS == 0][0] - csd[(OFFS >= 0) & (OFFS <= 6)].mean(),
                    "decrease_b_mean": csd[OFFS <= 0].mean() - csd[(OFFS >= 0) & (OFFS <= 6)].mean()})
    tab = pd.DataFrame(tab)
    print(f"band {band[0]}-{band[1]} min: {len(rates)} peaks of SPW-R rate from {len(set(x[0] for x in pk))} rats")
    print(tab.round(3).to_string())
    for col in ("decrease_a", "decrease_b", "decrease_a_mean", "decrease_b_mean"):
        rho = stats.spearmanr(tab[col], tab.median_rate)
        print(f"  {col}: top decile {tab[col].iloc[-1]:.3f}; Spearman with median rate rho = {rho.statistic:.3f}, p = {rho.pvalue:.3g}")

Result: not reproduced. Under neither band nor baseline is the decrease of phase dispersion correlated with SPW-R rate at p < 0.05: Spearman rho -0.24 (p = 0.51) for baseline (a) and 0.55 (p = 0.098) for baseline (b), the same in both bands. The decrease in the top decile is positive under all four readings (0.022 to 0.506), but it is positive in every decile, including the lowest (0.23 to 0.47). With the mean over 0 to +30 min in place of the minimum, rho is -0.19 to 0.56 (p = 0.09 to 0.86), and the top decile's decrease is negative with baseline (a).

edfig5-cross-frequency-coupling¶

SPW-R rate and glucose show power-power and phase-power coupling at periods of 15 to 75 min, with the faster SPW-R rhythm (about 40 min) modulating the slower glucose rhythm (about 60 min).

As the claims file: band-pass at log-spaced periods (here 12 to 120 min: a band centred at 10 min would sit at the Nyquist period of 5-min readings), Hilbert envelopes; power-power is the correlation of the SPW-R-rate and glucose envelopes for each pair of periods per rat, against 100 circular shuffles of SPW-R rate per rat, with a paired t-test across rats on the mean over 15 to 60 min. Phase-power is SPW-R rate (z-scored per rat) by glucose phase (the 15 to 75 min band), with a Rayleigh test of the rate-weighted phases pooled over rats (weights: z-scored rate minus its minimum, so that they are positive; a choice). Both signals are filtered only over stretches where both are recorded. The shortest stretch that is filtered is a choice: 12 h (six cycles of the longest period, 120 min) is the main reading, with 24 h and 6 h as variants. Bins are autocorrelated, so the pooled Rayleigh p is also compared with circular shifts of SPW-R rate.

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
PER = np.round(np.geomspace(12, 120, 12), 1)
def comod(eg, er):
    out = np.full((len(PER), len(PER)), np.nan)
    for i in range(len(PER)):
        for j in range(len(PER)):
            ok = np.isfinite(eg[i]) & np.isfinite(er[j])
            if ok.sum() > 50:
                out[i, j] = np.corrcoef(eg[i][ok], er[j][ok])[0, 1]
    return out

def both_segments(b):
    """Rows with both SPW-R rate and delta current, renumbered into runs of consecutive readings."""
    ok = np.isfinite(b.rate.values) & np.isfinite(b.delta.values)
    c = b[ok].copy()
    pos = np.flatnonzero(ok)
    c["run"] = np.cumsum(np.r_[True, (np.diff(pos) != 1) | (c.run.values[1:] != c.run.values[:-1])])
    return c

patch = (PER >= 15) & (PER <= 60)

def rayleigh_w(ph, z):
    """Resultant length of phases weighted by z minus its minimum, and the Rayleigh p for n phases."""
    w = z - z.min()
    Rw = np.abs(np.sum(w * np.exp(1j * ph))) / w.sum()
    n = len(ph)
    return Rw, np.exp(np.sqrt(1 + 4 * n + 4 * (n ** 2 - (n * Rw) ** 2)) - (1 + 2 * n))

def coupling(min_len, show_matrix=False):
    """Power-power and phase-power coupling over stretches of at least min_len bins with both signals."""
    obs_m, sh_m, rats5, mats, hrs5 = [], [], [], [], {}
    for s in RATS:
        b = both_segments(SUBJ[s]["b"])
        eg = np.array([band_phase(b, max(p / 1.25, 10.5), p * 1.25, col="delta", min_len=min_len)[1] for p in PER])
        if np.all(np.isnan(eg)):
            continue
        er = np.array([band_phase(b, max(p / 1.25, 10.5), p * 1.25, col="rate", min_len=min_len)[1] for p in PER])
        hrs5[s] = round(float(np.isfinite(eg[0]).sum()) * 5 / 60, 1)
        M = comod(eg, er)
        sh = []
        for i in range(100):
            sb = S.circular_shuffle(b, rng)
            esh = np.array([band_phase(sb, max(p / 1.25, 10.5), p * 1.25, col="rate", min_len=min_len)[1] for p in PER])
            sh.append(np.nanmean(comod(eg, esh)[np.ix_(patch, patch)]))
        rats5.append(s); mats.append(M); obs_m.append(np.nanmean(M[np.ix_(patch, patch)])); sh_m.append(np.mean(sh))
    obs_m, sh_m = np.array(obs_m), np.array(sh_m)
    t = stats.ttest_rel(obs_m, sh_m)
    print(f"--- stretches of at least {min_len * 5 / 60:.0f} h with both SPW-R rate and delta current: {len(rats5)} rats; hours used per rat: {hrs5}")
    print(f"power-power, mean over 15-60 min: observed {obs_m.mean():.3f} (per rat {np.round(obs_m, 3)}), shuffled {sh_m.mean():.3f}; paired t = {t.statistic:.2f}, p = {t.pvalue:.2g}")
    MM = np.nanmean(mats, axis=0)
    i, j = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(MM), MM.shape)
    off = np.nanmean([MM[a, c] for a in range(len(PER)) for c in range(len(PER)) if a > c])
    below = np.nanmean([MM[a, c] for a in range(len(PER)) for c in range(len(PER)) if a < c])
    print(f"mean comodulogram peak R = {MM[i, j]:.3f} at glucose period {PER[i]} min and SPW-R period {PER[j]} min; "
          f"mean R with glucose period longer than SPW-R period {off:.3f}, shorter {below:.3f}, diagonal {np.nanmean(np.diag(MM)):.3f}")
    if show_matrix:
        print(pd.DataFrame(MM, index=[f"glu {p}" for p in PER], columns=[f"spw {p}" for p in PER]).round(2).to_string())
    # phase-power: glucose phase (15-75 min band) and z-scored SPW-R rate, pooled over rats
    ph_all, z_all, segs5, per_rat_p = [], [], [], {}
    for s in rats5:
        b = both_segments(SUBJ[s]["b"])
        ph, _ = band_phase(b, 15, 75, min_len=min_len)
        ok = np.isfinite(ph)
        b = b[ok].assign(ph=ph[ok])
        b["z"] = (b.rate - b.rate.mean()) / b.rate.std()
        ph_all.append(b.ph.values); z_all.append(b.z.values); segs5.append(b)
        per_rat_p[s] = rayleigh_w(b.ph.values, b.z.values)[1]
    ph_all = np.concatenate(ph_all); z_all = np.concatenate(z_all); w = z_all - z_all.min()
    Rw, p_ray = rayleigh_w(ph_all, z_all)
    mean_phase = np.degrees(np.angle(np.sum(w * np.exp(1j * ph_all))))
    print(f"phase-power: {len(ph_all)} bins; weighted resultant length {Rw:.4f}, Rayleigh p = {p_ray:.3g}, preferred glucose phase {mean_phase:.0f} deg")
    # null for the pooled resultant length: SPW-R rate circularly shifted within each stretch (bins are autocorrelated)
    null = np.array([rayleigh_w(ph_all, np.concatenate([S.circular_shuffle(b, rng, x="z").z.values for b in segs5]))[0] for i in range(200)])
    print(f"   circular-shift null of the resultant length (200): 95th percentile {np.percentile(null, 95):.4f}; share >= observed {np.mean(null >= Rw):.3f}")
    print(f"   per-rat weighted Rayleigh p < 0.05 in {sum(p < 0.05 for p in per_rat_p.values())} of {len(per_rat_p)} rats")
    pb = pd.cut(ph_all, np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 13))
    print("   mean z-scored SPW-R rate by glucose phase:", pd.Series(z_all).groupby(pb, observed=True).mean().round(3).values)

for min_len, show in ((288, False), (144, True), (72, False)):
    coupling(min_len, show)

Result: partially reproduced. Over stretches of at least 12 h with both signals (16 rats), power-power coupling over 15 to 60 min exceeds the shuffles (mean R 0.064 against -0.007, paired t = 2.57, p = 0.021), and the rate-weighted glucose phases are non-uniform (Rayleigh p = 3.2e-09, resultant length 0.033, above all 200 circular shifts, whose 95th percentile is 0.013; p < 0.05 in 10 of 16 rats singly). The comodulogram peak (R 0.216) lies on the diagonal, at 79.0 min for both signals, so the third condition, a peak at a longer glucose period, fails; the mean correlation where the glucose period is longer than the SPW-R period (below the diagonal of the printed matrix) is 0.072 against 0.047 where it is shorter. With 6-h stretches the result is the same (p = 0.025 and 1.1e-08, peak at 79.0 min for both). With 24-h stretches only 3 rats remain and neither test reaches p < 0.05 (p = 0.24 and 0.82). The paper's p bounds (1e-24, 1e-18) are not reached.

edfig1-glucose-rhythm¶

Interstitial glucose fluctuations show an approximately 60-min oscillation, with power elevated above a linear best fit to the spectrum at periods of 15 to 90 min.

As Extended Data Fig. 1g-i: power spectral density of delta current per rat (Welch, 24-h segments within runs, a standard choice), a line fitted on log-log axes (the claims file's standard choice) and subtracted, averaged across rats; and the mean autocorrelogram of delta current. All subjects with at least one 24-h run of readings are used (the glucose series do not need the electrophysiology). The legend says "linear best fit" without the axes, so the fit is also run on semi-log and linear axes (power normalized per subject), over the whole spectrum or over 10 to 300 min, and with 12-h segments.

for s in sorted(SUBJ):
    glu = SUBJ[s]["glu"].copy()
    glu["delta"] = np.where(glu.run.eq(glu.run.shift(1)), glu.nA.diff(), np.nan)
    segs = [g.delta.values[1:] for _, g in glu.groupby("run") if len(g) >= 289]
    if not segs:
        continue

        f, p = signal.welch(np.nan_to_num(x), fs=FS, nperseg=288)
        ps.append(p * len(x))

# variants: axes of the line, the range it is fitted over, and the segment length
def spectra(nper):
    out = []
    for s in sorted(SUBJ):
        glu = SUBJ[s]["glu"].copy()
        glu["delta"] = np.where(glu.run.eq(glu.run.shift(1)), glu.nA.diff(), np.nan)
        segs = [g.delta.values[1:] for _, g in glu.groupby("run") if len(g) >= nper + 1]
        if segs:
            ps = [signal.welch(np.nan_to_num(x), fs=FS, nperseg=nper)[1] * len(x) for x in segs]
            out.append(np.sum(ps, axis=0) / sum(len(x) for x in segs))
    return signal.welch(np.zeros(nper), fs=FS, nperseg=nper)[0], out

rows = []
for nper, seg in ((288, "24 h"), (144, "12 h")):
    fq, P = spectra(nper)
    F, per = fq[1:], 1 / fq[1:] / 60
    for axes in ("log-log", "semi-log (log power)", "linear"):
        for frange in ("all", "10-300 min"):
            sel = np.ones(len(F), bool) if frange == "all" else (per >= 10) & (per <= 300)
            res = []
            for p in P:
                y = p[1:] / p[1:].sum()
                X = np.log10(F) if axes == "log-log" else F
                Y = y if axes == "linear" else np.log10(y)
                res.append(Y - np.polyval(np.polyfit(X[sel], Y[sel], 1), X))
            m = np.mean(res, axis=0)
            win = (per >= 10) & (per <= 300)
            b15 = (per >= 15) & (per <= 90)
            rows.append({"segment": seg, "axes": axes, "fit_over": frange, "subjects": len(P),
                         "peak_period_min": per[np.argmax(np.where(win, m, -np.inf))],
                         "positive_15_90": f"{int((m[b15] > 0).sum())} of {int(b15.sum())}",
                         "shortest_positive_period": per[win & (m > 0)].min() if np.any(win & (m > 0)) else np.nan,
                         "peak_in_54_66": 54 <= per[np.argmax(np.where(win, m, -np.inf))] <= 66})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(1).to_string())

Result: not reproduced. In 25 subjects the power of delta current above a log-log linear fit is elevated from about 22 to 131 min, with its peak at 51.4 min (per subject 32 to 60 min), outside 60 +- 6 min; below 22 min the residual is negative, so it is positive at only 51 of the 81 frequencies between 15 and 90 min. The mean autocorrelogram has its first side peak at 70 min with a value of 0.013, also outside the tolerance. Neither condition holds under any of the 12 variants of axes, fit range and segment length: the residual peak lies at 43.6 to 51.4 min (log-log), 10.1 min (semi-log) or 68.6 to 72.0 min (linear), and the residual is negative somewhere between 15 and 90 min in every variant. The spectrum has a broad hump of excess power from about 22 to 131 min, but the autocorrelogram shows no rhythm at its peak: it is -0.06 at a 50-min lag, and its first side peak, at 70 min, is 0.013. Neither the expected period nor the 15 to 90 min range is matched.

edfig1-glucose-circadian-meals¶

Glucose concentrations are modulated over the circadian cycle and rise after meals.

The meal times of the fasting experiment are not in the dandiset, so the meal part and its expected values (36 meals, 4 rats) cannot be tested. The circadian part of the criterion is run: current by hour of day averaged per subject, one-way ANOVA of hour on the hourly means pooled over subjects.

In [19]:
hourly = []
for s in sorted(SUBJ):
    glu = SUBJ[s]["glu"]
    h = S.clock(SUBJ[s]["ref"], glu.t).hour
    m = glu.nA.groupby(h).mean()
    if len(m) == 24:
        hourly.append(pd.DataFrame({"subject": s, "hour": m.index, "nA": m.values}))
hourly = pd.concat(hourly)
an = stats.f_oneway(*[g.nA.values for _, g in hourly.groupby("hour")])
print(f"{hourly.subject.nunique()} subjects; one-way ANOVA of hour of day: F = {an.statistic:.2f}, p = {an.pvalue:.3g}")
print("mean current by hour (nA):", hourly.groupby("hour").nA.mean().round(1).to_dict())
# variant within rats: the linear decay of each run of at least 24 h removed, then each subject's mean
hw = []
for s in sorted(SUBJ):
    glu = SUBJ[s]["glu"].copy()
    glu = glu[glu.groupby("run").t.transform("size") >= 288].copy()
    if not len(glu):
        continue
    glu["resid"] = glu.groupby("run").nA.transform(lambda x: x - np.polyval(np.polyfit(np.arange(len(x)), x.values, 1), np.arange(len(x))))
    m = glu.resid.groupby(S.clock(SUBJ[s]["ref"], glu.t).hour).mean()
    if len(m) == 24:
        hw.append(pd.DataFrame({"subject": s, "hour": m.index, "nA": m.values - m.mean()}))
hw = pd.concat(hw)
an2 = stats.f_oneway(*[g.nA.values for _, g in hw.groupby("hour")])
fr = stats.friedmanchisquare(*[g.sort_values("subject").nA.values for _, g in hw.groupby("hour")])
print(f"within subjects, decay removed: {hw.subject.nunique()} subjects; one-way ANOVA F = {an2.statistic:.2f}, p = {an2.pvalue:.3g}; "
      f"Friedman chi2 = {fr.statistic:.1f}, p = {fr.pvalue:.3g}")
print("mean deviation by hour (nA):", hw.groupby("hour").nA.mean().round(2).to_dict())

Result: blocked (meal times are not in the dandiset). The circadian part of the criterion does not find a modulation: one-way ANOVA of hour of day on the hourly means of 25 subjects, F = 0.46, p = 0.99; the mean current ranges from 28.6 nA (06:00 to 07:00) to 31.3 nA (20:00). The criterion's test pools hourly means across subjects whose offsets differ by tens of nA. Within subjects, with each run's linear decay and each subject's mean removed, hour of day is significant (one-way ANOVA p = 0.024, Friedman p = 5.2e-05; lowest at 06:00 to 07:00, -0.84 nA, and highest at 13:00 to 14:00, +0.65 nA), so a circadian modulation is present in that variant, which the criterion does not use.

edfig1-sensor-decay¶

The raw sensor current decays slowly over days after implantation, while the magnitude of its fluctuations (delta current) stays stable.

Per placement, daily mean current and daily mean absolute delta current against day since the first reading (claims file). A placement is a run of consecutive readings lasting at least 3 days (a standard choice); slopes are compared as fractions of the first-day value.

In [20]:
rows = []
for s in sorted(SUBJ):
    glu = SUBJ[s]["glu"]
    for r, g in glu.groupby("run"):
        if len(g) < 3 * 288:
            continue
        day = ((g.t - g.t.iloc[0]) // 86400).astype(int)
        ad = g.nA.diff().abs()
        dm = g.nA.groupby(day).mean(); da = ad.groupby(day).mean()
        full = g.groupby(day).size() >= 144
        dm, da = dm[full], da[full]
        sl_c = np.polyfit(dm.index, dm.values, 1)[0]; sl_d = np.polyfit(da.index, da.values, 1)[0]
        rows.append({"subject": s, "run": r, "days": len(dm), "first_day_nA": dm.iloc[0], "slope_nA_per_day": sl_c,
                     "rel_slope_current": sl_c / dm.iloc[0], "first_day_abs_delta": da.iloc[0], "rel_slope_abs_delta": sl_d / da.iloc[0]})
dec = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(dec.round(3).to_string())
print(f"placements: {len(dec)} from {dec.subject.nunique()} subjects; current slope negative in {int((dec.slope_nA_per_day < 0).sum())}; "
      f"|relative slope of |delta|| smaller than that of the current in {int((dec.rel_slope_abs_delta.abs() < dec.rel_slope_current.abs()).sum())}")
print(f"median relative slope per day: current {dec.rel_slope_current.median():.3f}, |delta| {dec.rel_slope_abs_delta.median():.3f}")

supp-ripple-rate¶

CA1 SPW-Rs occur at 9.5 (+- 8.2) per minute on average, about 14,000 per day, ranging from none for several minutes to more than 40 in a minute.

SPW-R count in 1-min bins over all CA1 recording (minutes fully covered by a file with a CA1 SPW-R table). Readings for the rats: (a) every rat with CA1 SPW-Rs and glucose together, (b) the ripple and glucose cohort, of which only CGM1 is labelled in the files. All subjects with a CA1 table are also shown.

In [21]:
def minute_counts(d):
    out = []
    for x, y in d["iv"]:
        edges = np.arange(np.ceil(x / 60) * 60, y + 1e-9, 60)
        if len(edges) < 2:
            continue
        e = d["ev"].t.values
        out.append(np.diff(np.searchsorted(e, edges)))
    return np.concatenate(out) if out else np.array([], int)

MC = {s: minute_counts(SUBJ[s]) for s in SUBJ if SUBJ[s]["ev"] is not None}
rows = [{"subject": s, "minutes": len(c), "mean_per_min": c.mean(), "sd_per_min": c.std(), "max_per_min": c.max(),
         "per_day": c.mean() * 1440, "zero_runs_ge_5min": int(np.sum(np.diff(np.flatnonzero(np.diff(np.r_[1, (c == 0).astype(int), 1]))) [::2] >= 5))}
        for s, c in MC.items()]
mr = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(mr.round(2).to_string())
for name, keep in (("a: rats with SPW-Rs and glucose", RATS), ("b: CGM1", ["CGM1"]), ("all subjects with a CA1 table", list(MC))):
    c = np.concatenate([MC[s] for s in keep])
    print(f"{name}: {len(keep)} rats, {len(c) / 60:.0f} h; mean {c.mean():.2f} (sd {c.std():.2f}) per minute, {c.mean() * 1440:.0f} per day, "
          f"max {c.max()} per minute; mean of rat means {mr[mr.subject.isin(keep)].mean_per_min.mean():.2f}")
    c5 = np.concatenate([minute_counts({"iv": SUBJ[s]["iv"], "ev": SUBJ[s]["ev_all"]}) for s in keep])
    print(f"   variant, all stored events (no 5 s.d. threshold): mean {c5.mean():.2f} per minute, {c5.mean() * 1440:.0f} per day, max {c5.max()}")

supp-ripples-stable-across-days¶

In each rat the shape, amplitude and rate of SPW-Rs are consistent across days.

Per rat and calendar day (days with at least 6 h of CA1 recording, a standard choice), the median amplitude (peak_normed_power, the Methods' maximum normalized squared signal; peak_amplitude shown as a variant), median duration and mean rate; Spearman correlation with day, and whether every daily value stays within 20% of the rat's overall median (claims file).

In [22]:
from itertools import permutations

def spearman_exact_p(y):
    """Two-sided exact p of Spearman's rho with day order, over all orderings (up to 8 days)."""
    n = len(y)
    if n > 8:
        return np.nan
    r = stats.rankdata(y); r = r - r.mean()
    d = np.arange(n) - (n - 1) / 2
    null = np.abs(r[np.array(list(permutations(range(n))))] @ d)
    return float(np.mean(null >= abs(r @ d) - 1e-9))

rows = []
for s, d in SUBJ.items():
    if d["ev"] is None:
        continue
    e = d["ev"].copy(); e["day"] = S.clock(d["ref"], e.t).normalize()
    secs = pd.Series(np.concatenate([np.arange(x, y, 60) for x, y in d["iv"]]))
    mins_per_day = S.clock(d["ref"], secs).normalize().value_counts()
    good = mins_per_day[mins_per_day >= 360].index
    g = e[e.day.isin(good)].groupby("day")
    daily = pd.DataFrame({"amp": g.peak_normed_power.median(), "amp_uV": g.peak_amplitude.median(),
                          "dur": g.duration.median(), "rate": g.size() / mins_per_day[good].reindex(g.size().index)})
    if len(daily) < 3:
        continue
    row = {"subject": s, "days": len(daily)}
    for k in daily:
        rho = stats.spearmanr(np.arange(len(daily)), daily[k])
        med = e[k if k not in ("amp", "amp_uV", "dur") else {"amp": "peak_normed_power", "amp_uV": "peak_amplitude", "dur": "duration"}[k]].median() if k != "rate" else daily[k].median()
        row[f"{k}_rho"] = rho.statistic; row[f"{k}_p"] = rho.pvalue; row[f"{k}_p_exact"] = spearman_exact_p(daily[k].values)
        row[f"{k}_within20"] = bool(np.all(np.abs(daily[k] / med - 1) <= 0.2))
        row[f"{k}_maxdev"] = float(np.max(np.abs(daily[k] / med - 1)))
    rows.append(row)
st = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(st.round(3).to_string())
for k in ("amp", "amp_uV", "dur", "rate"):
    ok = (st[f"{k}_p"] >= 0.05) | st[f"{k}_within20"]
    print(f"{k}: consistent (Spearman p >= 0.05 or within 20%) in {int(ok.sum())} of {len(st)} rats; "
          f"within 20% in {int(st[f'{k}_within20'].sum())}; Spearman p < 0.05 in {int((st[f'{k}_p'] < 0.05).sum())} "
          f"(exact p < 0.05 in {int((st[f'{k}_p_exact'] < 0.05).sum())} of {int(st[f'{k}_p_exact'].notna().sum())} rats with up to 8 days)")
print("exact two-sided p of a perfectly monotone series, by number of days:", {n: float(f"{spearman_exact_p(np.arange(n)):.2g}") for n in range(3, 9)})

Result: reproduced. Daily median amplitude (peak normed power) and duration show no trend with day (no Spearman p < 0.05) in all 15 rats with at least 3 days, and the daily rate in 11 of 15 (13 counting rats whose rate stays within 20%). Amplitude stays within 20% of the median in only 5 rats, and the rate in 4, so the consistency rests mostly on the absence of trends. Amplitude in microvolts trends with day in 5 rats. These p values are scipy's asymptotic ones, which are too small with few days: every perfectly monotone series of 3 or 4 days gets p = 0.000, where the exact two-sided p is 0.33 for 3 days and 0.083 for 4, so with 3 or 4 days no series can reach p < 0.05. With exact p no rat with up to 8 days has a trend in any measure: the two rate trends that fail the criterion (CGM2, 5 days, rho 0.9, exact p 0.083; CGM52, 4 days, exact p 0.083) and the microvolt trends of CGM46, CGM51 and Vanessa are artefacts of the asymptotic p. With exact p the rate is consistent in all 15 rats, and amplitude in microvolts trends only in CGM1 and CGM31 (12 and 18 days). In CGM30 the median peak_amplitude over all events is 0, which makes its deviation infinite; this variant does not enter the criterion.

edfig3-ripple-rate-rhythms¶

SPW-R rate varies with circadian and ultradian rhythms, with spectral peaks at about 24 h and about 4 h, in 1,568.5 recording hours from 8 rats.

Power spectral density of SPW-R rate in 5-min bins per rat, averaged over rats (claims file). The recordings have gaps, so the spectrum is a Lomb-Scargle periodogram of the covered bins (a standard choice for unevenly sampled data). The 8 rats with the most CA1 recording are used, and all rats with at least 48 h as a variant.

In [23]:
per_h = np.linspace(1, 48, 400)
freqs = 2 * np.pi / (per_h * 3600)
LS, hrs = {}, {}
for s, d in SUBJ.items():
    if d["ev"] is None:
        continue
    t_all, r_all = [], []
    for x, y in d["iv"]:
        edges = np.arange(x, y - 299, 300)
        if len(edges) < 2:
            continue
        c = np.diff(np.searchsorted(d["ev"].t.values, np.r_[edges, edges[-1] + 300]))
        t_all.append(edges + 150); r_all.append(c / 5)
    t_all = np.concatenate(t_all); r_all = np.concatenate(r_all)
    hrs[s] = len(t_all) * 5 / 60
    if hrs[s] >= 48:
        p = signal.lombscargle(t_all, r_all - r_all.mean(), freqs, normalize=True)
        LS[s] = p
top8 = sorted(hrs, key=hrs.get, reverse=True)[:8]
print("CA1 recording hours per subject:", {k: round(v, 1) for k, v in sorted(hrs.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])})
for name, keep in (("8 rats with the most recording", top8), ("all rats with >= 48 h", list(LS))):
    m = np.mean([LS[s] for s in keep], axis=0)
    pk, _ = signal.find_peaks(m)
    order = pk[np.argsort(m[pk])[::-1]]
    print(f"{name}: {len(keep)} rats, {sum(hrs[s] for s in keep):.1f} h; local peaks (period h, power): "
          f"{[(round(per_h[i], 1), round(m[i], 4)) for i in order[:8]]}")
    prom = signal.peak_prominences(m, pk)[0]
    rank = pd.Series(prom).rank(ascending=False).values
    for target in (24, 4):
        k = np.argmin(np.abs(per_h[pk] - target))
        print(f"   peak nearest {target} h at {per_h[pk][k]:.1f} h: power {m[pk][k]:.4f}, prominence {prom[k]:.4f}, "
              f"rank {int(rank[k])} of {len(pk)} peaks by prominence (largest prominence {prom.max():.4f} at {per_h[pk][np.argmax(prom)]:.1f} h)")
    print(f"   peak nearest 24 h: {per_h[pk][np.argmin(np.abs(per_h[pk] - 24))]:.1f} h; nearest 4 h: {per_h[pk][np.argmin(np.abs(per_h[pk] - 4))]:.1f} h")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.plot(per_h, np.mean([LS[s] for s in top8], axis=0)); ax.set_xlabel("period (h)"); ax.set_ylabel("normalized power"); plt.show()

Result: partially reproduced. The mean Lomb-Scargle spectrum of the 8 rats with the most recording has local peaks at 24.0 h and 3.8 h, both inside the tolerances, but they are not its largest peaks (42.3 and 19.5 h are larger), and the 8 rats hold 1,889.8 h of recording, outside 1,568.5 +- 156.9 h. By prominence the 24.0-h peak ranks 4th of 45 local peaks and the 3.8-h peak 12th (prominence 0.0034 against 0.0175 for the 42.3-h peak), so on this 400-point grid a nearby local peak is weak evidence of a 4-h rhythm.

edfig2-refractory-period¶

Inter-ripple intervals drop to zero below about 20 ms, a refractory period between ripples, with peaks reflecting bursts of ripples.

Histogram of intervals between consecutive SPW-R peaks within a file, per rat, 1-ms bins (claims file); the shortest interval with counts. The legend does not name the time point of each event, so start-to-start and stop-to-stop intervals and the gap from one event's stop to the next one's start are shown as variants. The Methods' detector merges neighbouring events ("identify peaks above a threshold merging neighbouring events", SPW-R detection), which sets a floor on the gap.

Result: not reproduced. Between SPW-R peaks, the reading the criterion uses, the shortest interval is 28.8 to 39.2 ms (median 34.4 ms) and no interval below 20 ms occurs in any of 22 rats; no rat has its shortest interval in 18 to 22 ms. Start-to-start (median shortest 40.8 ms) does not match either. The gap from one event's stop to the next one's start has its minimum at exactly 20.0 ms in 19 rats and at 15.2 ms in CGM1, CGM2 and CGM3, so it lies in 18 to 22 ms in 19 of 22 rats. A floor at the same value in nearly every rat matches the merging of neighbouring events in the detection, so the 20-ms drop the legend describes may be this rule, measured as stop to start.

edfig4-nrem-wake¶

The SPW-R and glucose cross-correlogram does not differ between NREM sleep and waking, and its negative peak does not change across state transitions.

Sleep states are stored for six subjects; three of them (CGM1, CGM2, CGM3) have SPW-Rs and glucose together. As the claims file: blocks of 4 h; within each, the correlation at +10 min (Spearman, the correlation type under which the main claim matched) between the SPW-R rate of bins mostly in NREM (or mostly awake) and the delta current 10 min later; one value per block and state, unpaired two-sided t-test (per-rat means, paired, as a variant). Transitions: for each change from an awake to a NREM episode (and the reverse) where both episodes last at least 10 min (a choice), the most negative correlation from +5 to +20 min in the 2 h before and the 2 h after, paired t-test.

The main analysis pairs the SPW-R count and the glucose change of the same 5-min interval, as in fig2-ripple-rate-predicts-glucose (an assumption). The two alignments one reading apart are shown as variants: counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading, or taking the change to the next reading, which is the same as moving the offset by one reading.

In [25]:
def state_of_bins(b, ss):
    lab = np.full(len(b), "", dtype=object)
    for state in ("Non-REM", "Awake"):
        g = ss[ss.label == state]
        cov_ = S.coverage(list(zip(g.start, g.stop)), b.t.values - S.STEP, b.t.values)
        lab[cov_ > 0.5] = state
    return lab

def nrem_wake(k):
    blocks, trans = [], []
    for s in RATS:
        fs = SUBJ[s]["files"]
        if not any(f["sleep"] is not None and len(f["sleep"]) for f in fs):
            continue
        ss = pd.concat([f["sleep"] + [S.clock_offset(f, SUBJ[s]["ref"]), S.clock_offset(f, SUBJ[s]["ref"]), ""]
                        for f in fs if f["sleep"] is not None]).sort_values("start").reset_index(drop=True)
        b = SUBJ[s]["b"].copy()
        b["state"] = state_of_bins(b, ss)
        b["block"] = ((b.t - b.t.min()) // (4 * 3600)).astype(int)
        for blk, g in b.groupby("block"):
            for state in ("Non-REM", "Awake"):
                gg = g.copy(); gg.loc[gg.state != state, "rate"] = np.nan
                x, y = S.lagged_pairs(gg, 2 + k)
                if len(x) >= 10:
                    blocks.append({"rat": s, "block": blk, "state": state, "pairs": len(x), "R10": S._corr(x, y, "spearman")})
        # transitions between episodes of at least 10 min
        ss2 = ss[ss.label.isin(["Non-REM", "Awake"])].reset_index(drop=True)
        for i in range(1, len(ss2)):
            a, c = ss2.iloc[i - 1], ss2.iloc[i]
            if a.label == c.label or a.stop - a.start < 600 or c.stop - c.start < 600 or abs(c.start - a.stop) > 60:
                continue
            t0 = c.start
            vals = {}
            for side, (lo, hi) in (("before", (t0 - 7200, t0)), ("after", (t0, t0 + 7200))):
                g = b[(b.t > lo) & (b.t <= hi)]
                cc = [S._corr(*S.lagged_pairs(g, j + k), "spearman") for j in (1, 2, 3, 4)]
                vals[side] = np.nanmin(cc) if np.any(np.isfinite(cc)) else np.nan
            trans.append({"rat": s, "type": f"{a.label}->{c.label}", **vals})
    return pd.DataFrame(blocks), pd.DataFrame(trans)

blocks, trans = nrem_wake(0)
nrem = blocks[blocks.state == "Non-REM"].R10; wake = blocks[blocks.state == "Awake"].R10
nrem, wake = nrem.dropna(), wake.dropna()
t = stats.ttest_ind(nrem, wake)
print(f"blocks: NREM n = {len(nrem)}, mean R10 {nrem.mean():.3f}; awake n = {len(wake)}, mean {wake.mean():.3f}; unpaired t = {t.statistic:.2f}, p = {t.pvalue:.3g}")
pm = blocks.groupby(["rat", "state"]).R10.mean().unstack()
print(pm.round(3).to_string())
if len(pm) > 1:
    tp = stats.ttest_rel(pm["Non-REM"], pm["Awake"], nan_policy="omit"); print(f"per-rat means, paired: t = {tp.statistic:.2f}, p = {tp.pvalue:.3g}")
for typ, g in trans.dropna().groupby("type"):
    tt = stats.ttest_rel(g.before, g.after)
    print(f"{typ}: {len(g)} transitions from {g.rat.nunique()} rats; most negative R (+5 to +20 min) before {g.before.mean():.3f}, after {g.after.mean():.3f}; paired t = {tt.statistic:.2f}, p = {tt.pvalue:.3g}")
print("Alignment variants:")
for name, k in ALIGN.items():
    if k == 0:
        continue
    bl, tr = nrem_wake(k)
    n_, w_ = bl[bl.state == "Non-REM"].R10.dropna(), bl[bl.state == "Awake"].R10.dropna()
    txt = "; ".join(f"{typ}: {len(g)}, p = {stats.ttest_rel(g.before, g.after).pvalue:.3g}" for typ, g in tr.dropna().groupby("type"))
    print(f"   {name}: blocks NREM mean {n_.mean():.3f} (n = {len(n_)}), awake {w_.mean():.3f} (n = {len(w_)}), unpaired p = {stats.ttest_ind(n_, w_).pvalue:.3g}; transitions {txt}")

Result: reproduced, on 3 rats where the paper has 8, resting on the alignment assumption. NREM and awake blocks do not differ at p < 0.05 (mean R at +10 min -0.017 against -0.083, unpaired t p = 0.057; per-rat means paired p = 0.27), and the most negative correlation does not change across awake-to-NREM (p = 0.15, 13 transitions) or NREM-to-awake transitions (p = 0.23, 23 transitions from one rat). The awake blocks are more negative, near the threshold, and the test has little power with 3 rats. Under the alignments one reading apart, counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading makes the awake blocks differ from the NREM blocks (mean -0.109 against -0.043, unpaired p = 0.038), so the claim fails there; taking the change to the next reading, no test reaches p < 0.05 (blocks p = 0.21, transitions p = 0.27 and 0.66).

edfig4-no-hour-differs¶

No hour of the day has a significantly different SPW-R and glucose correlation than any other hour (smallest P = 0.53).

As the claims file: per rat, cross-correlograms in 4-h windows of the day centred on each hour (all days pooled), integrated over offsets +5 to +20 min (the sum of R at +5, +10, +15, +20 min; Spearman, as for the main claim); Student's t-test across rats for every pair of hours. Rats with at least 24 h of both signals (a standard choice, so that each hour has data). A rat-hour in which any of the four correlations cannot be computed is left out.

The main analysis pairs the SPW-R count and the glucose change of the same 5-min interval, as in fig2-ripple-rate-predicts-glucose (an assumption). The two alignments one reading apart are shown as variants: counting SPW-Rs over the 5 min after each reading, or taking the change to the next reading, which is the same as moving the offset by one reading.

In [26]:
rats24 = list(cov[cov.hours_with_both >= 24].subject)

def hour_matrix(k):
    """Integrated R (+5 to +20 min) per rat and hour of day, with the lags moved by k readings (the alignment)."""
    H = np.full((len(rats24), 24), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(rats24):
        b = SUBJ[s]["b"]
        hod = (b.clock.dt.hour + b.clock.dt.minute / 60).values
        for hcent in range(24):
            dist = np.abs(((hod - hcent) + 12) % 24 - 12)
            g = b.copy(); g.loc[dist > 2, "rate"] = np.nan
            v = [S._corr(*S.lagged_pairs(g, j + k), "spearman") for j in (1, 2, 3, 4)]
            H[i, hcent] = np.sum(v) if np.all(np.isfinite(v)) else np.nan
    return H

def hour_pairs(H):
    ps = []
    for a in range(24):
        for c in range(a + 1, 24):
            ps.append((a, c, stats.ttest_ind(H[:, a], H[:, c], nan_policy="omit").pvalue,
                       stats.ttest_rel(H[:, a], H[:, c], nan_policy="omit").pvalue))
    return pd.DataFrame(ps, columns=["hour_a", "hour_b", "p_student", "p_paired"])

H = hour_matrix(0)
ps = hour_pairs(H)
print(f"{len(rats24)} rats: {rats24}; rat-hours with no valid integrated correlation (left out): {int(np.isnan(H).sum())} of {H.size}")
print("integrated R (+5 to +20 min) by hour, mean over rats:", np.round(np.nanmean(H, axis=0), 3))
print(f"{len(ps)} pairs of hours; Student's t-test: smallest p = {ps.p_student.min():.3f}, pairs with p < 0.05: {int((ps.p_student < 0.05).sum())}; "
      f"paired variant: smallest p = {ps.p_paired.min():.3g}, pairs with p < 0.05: {int((ps.p_paired < 0.05).sum())}; "
      f"expected by chance at 0.05: {0.05 * len(ps):.1f}")
for name, k in ALIGN.items():
    if k:
        p_ = hour_pairs(hour_matrix(k))
        print(f"alignment variant, {name}: Student's t smallest p = {p_.p_student.min():.3f}, pairs with p < 0.05: {int((p_.p_student < 0.05).sum())}")

integrated R (+5 to +20 min) by hour, mean over rats: [-0.145 -0.199 -0.031 -0.036  0.017  0.048 -0.132 -0.198 -0.13  -0.223
 -0.109 -0.089 -0.267 -0.241 -0.235 -0.298 -0.283 -0.374 -0.453 -0.417

alignment variant, delta to the next reading: Student's t smallest p = 0.015, pairs with p < 0.05: 13

Result: not reproduced. Student's t-test across 12 rats finds 10 of 276 pairs of hours at p < 0.05 (smallest p = 0.010), where the paper reports a smallest P of 0.53; the paired variant finds 25. 3 of 288 rat-hours have no valid correlation and are left out. The integrated correlation is most negative from 17:00 to 21:00 (-0.37 to -0.51) and near zero from 02:00 to 05:00 (-0.04 to 0.05). Ten pairs is fewer than the 13.8 expected by chance among 276 uncorrected tests, so the difference from the paper lies in the smallest p, not in a clear effect of hour. The two other alignments give the same outcome: smallest p 0.032 (2 pairs at p < 0.05) counting SPW-Rs after each reading, and 0.015 (13 pairs) with the change to the next reading.

edfig9-dorsal-ventral¶

Dorsal and ventral CA1 SPW-Rs are only weakly correlated, and ventral SPW-Rs are significantly less correlated with glucose fluctuations than dorsal SPW-Rs, which match the earlier dorsal cohorts.

The dorsal and ventral rats are the three subjects with Dorsalripples and Ventralripples tables (CGM37, CGM48, Vanessa). The correlation of dorsal and ventral 5-min SPW-R rates is taken over the files holding both tables. The glucose comparison needs glucose recorded with the electrophysiology: CGM37 has none, CGM48 has 2.2 h (too little for a day of at least 4 h, printed below), and Vanessa has three such days, two of which give a correlation; per-day correlations at +10 min (Spearman) for dorsal and ventral SPW-Rs, paired (a) and unpaired (b) t-tests, and the dorsal values against the other rats' per-rat values (unpaired t-test).

Dorsal and ventral 5-min SPW-R rates are correlated with r = 0.13 (Vanessa), 0.44 (CGM37) and 0.83 (CGM48), below 0.5 in two of three rats. Only Vanessa has days with at least 4 h of glucose and both tables (three days, two of which give a correlation; CGM48 has 2.2 h in all, CGM37 none): dorsal 0.115 and 0.239, ventral -0.088 and 0.096 at +10 min, the ventral values more negative (paired p = 0.11), and Vanessa's dorsal values differ from the other rats' (p = 0.009). Vanessa's sensor reads a median of 0.25 nA, so its glucose series is doubtful.

Size of the predictor models (edfig6-ripple-rate-best-predictor, edfig6d-pairwise-predictors, edfig6ef-latent-variables)¶

Six of the seven predictors of the Methods (power spectrum slope, theta residual, theta/delta ratio, high-pass coherence between shanks, movement, and NREM or wake where no sleep states are stored) have to be computed from the LFP and the accelerometer over every hour with glucose. The LFP is stored in chunks of 707 samples by 32 channels (gzip), so even one channel means reading all 32. The cell below times the reading of 30 min of LFP and of accelerometer from each of 16 files, in 4 processes (the cores of the machine that runs the notebook) and in 16 (the reading waits on the network), and scales the wall time to all rats, to the 8 rats with the most hours (the legend's n is 8) and to the 3 rats whose brain state is stored (in the others it would first have to be scored).

In [28]:
a = assets[assets.path == "sub-CGM31/sub-CGM31_ses-CGM31-720um-210209-085741_ecephys.nwb"].iloc[0]
with S.open_h5(a.asset_id) as h:
    lfp = h["processing/ecephys/LFP/ElectricalSeriesLFP/data"]; acc = h["acquisition/Accelerometer/data"]
    print("LFP chunks", lfp.chunks, lfp.compression, "; accelerometer chunks", acc.chunks, acc.compression,
          f"at {h['acquisition/Accelerometer/starting_time'].attrs['rate']} Hz")
# 30 min of LFP and accelerometer from each of 16 files, read in 4 and then in 16 processes
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
pool = [f for f in kept if f["lfp_n"] / f["lfp_rate"] > 1800 and "Accelerometer" in f["acquisition"]]
pick = pool[:: max(1, len(pool) // 16)][:16]
ids = [assets.set_index("path").asset_id[f["path"]] for f in pick]
top8_both = cov.sort_values("hours_with_both", ascending=False).subject[:8].tolist()
sets = {"all 18 rats": RATS, "the 8 rats with the most hours of both": top8_both,
        "the 3 rats with stored sleep states and glucose (CGM1, CGM2, CGM3)": ["CGM1", "CGM2", "CGM3"]}
for procs in (4, 16):
    t0 = time.time()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(procs) as ex:
        res = np.array(list(ex.map(S.time_read, ids)))
    wall = time.time() - t0
    sec_per_h = wall / (len(ids) * 0.5)
    print(f"16 x 30 min in {procs} processes: {wall:.1f} s of wall time, {sec_per_h:.1f} s per hour of recording; "
          f"per piece LFP median {np.median(res[:, 0]):.1f} s (range {res[:, 0].min():.1f} to {res[:, 0].max():.1f}), "
          f"accelerometer median {np.median(res[:, 1]):.1f} s")
    for name, rs in sets.items():
        h_ = cov[cov.subject.isin(rs)].hours_with_both.sum()
        print(f"   {name}: {h_:.0f} h, reading alone about {h_ * sec_per_h / 60:.0f} min, against a notebook limit of 30 min")

Blocked claims¶

  • edfig3e-ca1-firing-decrease, edfig8-lateral-septum-rectified. No file holds spike units (data check). The lateral septum recordings of ref. 26 are on the lab's server, which is not a pinned public source.
  • edfig4-fasting-fed, edfig1-glucose-circadian-meals (meal part). Meal times are not in the dandiset.
  • edfig6-ripple-rate-best-predictor, edfig6d-pairwise-predictors, edfig6ef-latent-variables. The predictors have to be computed from the LFP and the accelerometer over every hour with glucose. The reading speed varies with the network: in the runs made for this attempt a single 30-min piece of LFP took from about 1 to 22 s, and once 106 s, so the printed values change from run to run. In 4 processes the reading alone came to 4.4 to 4.6 s per hour of recording in three runs: 126 to 130 min for all 18 rats, 107 to 110 min for the 8 rats with the most hours and 41 to 42 min for the 3 rats with stored brain states. In 16 processes it came to 2.8 to 3.0 s per hour: 81 to 85 min for all rats, 69 to 72 min for the 8 rats and 26 to 28 min for the 3 rats, against the 30-min limit of a notebook. For the 3 rats the computation of the seven predictors and the 100 splits of each model at 41 offsets would come on top of the reading, and the result would cover 3 of the paper's 8 rats; a test on them is an analysis not run in this attempt. The brain state of the other 15 rats would first have to be scored.
  • fig3d-induced-ripples-lower-glucose, fig3-induced-effect-size, fig3ef-stimulation-dose-response, fig3f-stimulation-vs-shuffle, edfig7ab-stimulation-protocol, edfig7jm-induced-ripples-decoupled, edfig7-ppc-stimulation-no-effect. No file holds stimulation times or a stimulation channel, and no subject is labelled as optogenetic or PPC.
  • fig4-cno-controls-no-change, fig4-ls-dreadd-decouples, fig4-ls-dreadd-chance-level, fig4e-dreadd-time-course, fig4c-medial-septum-no-effect, edfig10-expression-correlates-effect. The recordings of the DREADD rats may be among the files, but nothing says which subjects had hM4Di in the lateral or medial septum or no virus, which days were CNO or vehicle days, or when the injections were given. The histology scores of Extended Data Fig. 10e are printed only in the figure.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's: 18 rats in place of 30; the glucose dates of twelve subjects were repaired; SPW-Rs are the stored events with a peak of at least 5 s.d.; the correlation type, the delta current filter, the unit of analysis and the lag range are open in the paper and were run under every reading the claims file lists; reading (a) of the rats cannot leave out CNO days or stimulation periods, which are not labelled; the coupling analysis filters stretches of at least 12 h with both signals. The SPW-R count of a 5-min interval is paired with the glucose change over the same interval, an assumption: under the alignments one reading apart the outcomes of fig2-ripple-rate-predicts-glucose, fig2g-clustered-ripples, edfig4-ripple-features and edfig4-nrem-wake change under one of the two, while those of fig2ef-correlation-beyond-shuffle and edfig4-no-hour-differs do not.

What was found about the dataset: the glucose timestamps of twelve subjects carry dates with day and month swapped; 27 recordings are deposited twice; the SPW-R peak column is relative to the file while start_time is on the session clock; several SPW-R tables were made with a 4 s.d. threshold where the Methods give 5; the session reference times are local wall-clock times labelled UTC; there is no mapping from subjects to the paper's rats or cohorts, and no stimulation, injection, meal or unit data; in four subjects the glucose and the electrophysiology cover different days; the detection parameters are not stored with the SPW-R tables, and the gap from one stored event's end to the next one's start is at least 20.0 ms in 19 rats and 15.2 ms in three.
